blocks.p: There are two forms of self-regulation: Active and Received.

Active Self-Regulation is what you do. You consciously anchor into safety and connect directly with defense. Skills like [Balancing and Pendulating](piece:balancing-and-pendulating) are your guide to Active self-regulation. You will notice specific moments of self-regulation during your intentional efforts, and this will pay off as a stronger Safety Baseline and reduced defensive activation in your daily life. Active self-regulation strengthens your vagal brake, builds capacity, and creates the conditions for a deeper level of regulation.

Received self-regulation is what becomes available through your Active self-regulation efforts. Received is not something you actively do. Received is what happens through you when your nervous system makes spontaneous shifts toward regulation. Your breath deepens on its own. Stuck sensations release. Impulses surface and complete. Received Self-Regulation is your body's processes taking over, but it can only emerge after you've done the Active work.
Put simply: practice Active Self-Regulation consistently, and Received Self-Regulation will open up when your system is ready.

Picture where practice takes you. You've built capacity. The skills are second nature. You can anchor in safety without thinking. You can Witness and Experience defensive activation with curiosity. You can Pendulate between safety and defense, and stay present with what arises. Your vagal brake has strengthened through countless practice sessions. You're nearing Received self-regulation.

Throughout the Skills Sequence, you actively practiced self-regulation. You intentionally and consciously applied the skills and saw benefits. Your Safety Baseline has risen and holds. You've also noticed a decrease in defensive activation and an increase in regulated mobility. While your stuck state isn't a significant hindrance to your daily functioning, self-regulation can go further.

Now, in Received Self-Regulation, you will continue to stay aware of the present moment and internal experiences, but step back from active doing and become more receptive to what the body needs. The body's natural wisdom takes over, shifting states, releasing what's stuck, and climbing the Polyvagal ladder toward safety and connection.

This might be the most important distinction: Received Self-Regulation is not something you do. It's something you allow. Received Self-Regulation occurs when you've completed all the preparation and your body finally has the safety, permission, and capacity to self-regulate. It's the shift from "I'm doing this" to "This is happening through me."

Your role changes. You are no longer the practitioner actively working through steps. Instead, you become the conduit for self-regulation. You stay present, stay curious, and remain anchored in safety as your body does what it needs to do.

Think of it this way: it's like the difference between rowing a boat and sailing. Rowing requires constant effort. You propel the boat with your own actions. Sailing requires skill and focus, but the wind does the work. You adjust the sails, steer, and stay alert, but the movement comes from something beyond your direct control. Received Self-Regulation is when the wind catches your sails.

The signs of Received Self-Regulation all center on anchored spontaneity. During your meditation practices with the Skills Sequence, you probably noticed Obstacles arising. Yes, these are spontaneous, in a sense. However, Obstacles are often predictable and indicate emerging dysregulation. So they are not what I mean by "anchored spontaneity."

When firmly anchored in safety and with a strong vagal brake, spontaneous shifts may occur. These are deep, organismic bodily processes that manifest as various SSIECs. Since your safety state is active, these spontaneous experiences won't be felt as defense. Instead, they are simply biological events happening in the present. A moment of fact and wonderment, not fear or hesitancy.

Received Self-Regulation can lead to spontaneous State shifts. These are conscious experiences of your Polyvagal state changing in real time. Examples include aggression or feelings of power as you move out of shutdown, an impulse to run when exiting fight, or the urge to hug a loved one after shifting out of flight. Spontaneous State shifts are noticeable through how they manifest as Sensations, Impulses, Emotions, and Cognitions.

Spontaneous Sensations also arise through Received Self-Regulation. Examples include tingling in your arms, warmth spreading through your chest, or a wave moving through your body. Sometimes they're the first sign that your body is trying to change state, but they can also be the experience of your current state. Regardless, be with them mindfully.

Along with spontaneous Sensations, spontaneous Impulses may also occur. For example, an urge to squeeze your fists, take a deeper breath, or stretch. These may be accompanied by physical releases: tears falling without you choosing to cry, a sigh escaping, or your body trembling or shuddering. More on this in [Impulses](piece:impulses).

Emotions softening or transforming naturally is another sign of anchored spontaneity. You've likely already noticed Emotions softening or new ones emerging as Obstacles through your practices. Spontaneous Emotions are similar, though they can feel like a seamless flow, one into the next, as your body processes and climbs the Polyvagal Ladder. Instead of using the Skills Sequence and intentionally applying the steps for each new Emotion, you're simply with them as they come and go.

Finally, spontaneous Cognitions. While practicing, an idea comes to mind to reach out to a loved one, indicating increased safety activation and an impulse to connect. Or an image of curling up on a couch may indicate a shutdown impulse to immobilize. You may think of something you need to get done or are now ready to start, stemming from the body filling with anchored mobilization in the form of play, productivity, or creativity. The past now makes sense, and how it connects to the present becomes clear. Old memories come to mind, or there's a newfound sense of belonging as a tiny piece of an infinite universe.
So, if Received Self-Regulation happens through you rather than something you actively do, what exactly is your role?

You are the Mindful Conduit. You create the conditions, stay present, and allow your body's wisdom to unfold. Even during the deepest meditation sessions, you remain consciously aware, even if you're not directing as you did during the Active Self-Regulation phase while using the Skills Sequence.

Let's revisit a metaphor I mentioned earlier: Active and Received Self-Regulation are like the difference between rowing a boat and sailing. Rowing requires constant effort. You move the boat through your actions. Achieving a healthy, noticeable level of self-regulation comes from your intentional efforts, creating a strong new Safety Baseline.

Sailing still requires skill and focus, but the wind does the work. You're adjusting the sails, steering, and staying present, yet the movement stems from something beyond your direct control. The same is true at even the deepest levels of meditation. You're still conscious. You remain aware of what's happening inside you. There are still words in your mind. But you can consciously choose to follow a Cognition, Emotion, Sensation, or Impulse, just as a sailor might decide to follow the wind. (I actually don't know anything about sailing, but this sounds accurate.)

Acting as the conduit for Received Self-Regulation is a deeply mindful process. It's one of presence without striving, of noticing without grasping. Imagine yourself in a quiet garden, drawn to a stunning rose in full bloom. Its petals, a vibrant tapestry of reds and pinks, catch the light in ways you've never quite seen. You lean closer. The fragrance envelops you, sweet and alive. Your senses awaken fully: the delicate curve of each petal, the play of shadow and sunlight across its face, the subtle color variations. You are completely absorbed, yet completely yourself. Your mind is quiet yet alert. You're not trying to understand the rose. You're simply with it, allowing it to reveal itself to you moment by moment.

In Received self-regulation, you're neither passive nor forceful. You're anchored and awake, intimately connected with your internal experience yet maintaining a clear sense of self, observing it all. Just as you might suddenly notice, "Wow, I never realized how incredible this flower is," you can also discover within yourself: "Wow, I never knew there was such a rich, complex universe happening inside me."

At this point, you may be thinking, "Justin… I hate to break it to you, but you're sounding rather woo-woo to me." I don't fault you for thinking that. If you haven't reached this depth of meditation, yes, it does sound rather woo-woo. I agree. I hope you put all of this into practice, remain patient, and experience Received self-regulation for yourself.
Let's discuss what you can actively do during Received Self-Regulation and what your overall goal is.

ol: Stay anchored in safety. This is always, always the top priority. Self-regulation works only when you are sufficiently anchored in your safety state. If you lose that connection, regulation stops, and dysregulation may begin. During any meditation, check in: "Am I still anchored? Do I still have access to safety? Can I connect with my breath? Can I still feel my safety cues?" If the answer is yes, keep going. If not, it's time to pause, re-anchor, and return when you're ready.

Stay grounded and curious without trying to control. You're interested in what's happening and in your internal experience, but you don't try to direct it or make it go a certain way. You're not thinking, "Okay, now I need to discharge this freeze energy" or "I should be feeling anger right now." Instead, you're asking yourself, "What's happening? What's here? What wants to emerge?" Curiosity keeps you present and engaged, while trying to control can suppress self-regulation. Keep curiosity alive.

As you're curious and exploring what's inside, follow rather than lead. Your body knows what to do. Your role is to follow its guidance. If an Impulse arises, follow it. If a Sensation appears, stay with it. If an Emotion shifts, go along with it. If a Cognition comes to consciousness, notice it. You're not deciding what should happen next. You're observing what is happening and staying present with it.

Your body knows what to do, so trust it. It has always aimed to self-regulate and is naturally wired for it. What's been missing is the safety, permission, and capacity to let it. You've built all of that through your practice. Now, trust that your body knows exactly what to do. It's okay to explicitly remind yourself, "My body can handle this."

Since your body can handle it, you can choose to intentionally allow self-regulation. Being the Mindful Conduit is not passive. It's active receptivity, a conscious choice to let things be as they are and to allow what wants to emerge. You're still using the A->W->E process, but you're fully engaged in the experience, not just going through the steps. You're not forcing, pushing, or trying to make something happen. You're also not checked out or dissociated. You're fully present, fully engaged, and fully allowing. Allowing sounds like: "Yes, you can be here." "I'm staying with you." "I'm not going to make you go away." "Show me what you need."

As you stay with what surfaces, you will also stay connected to your breath. Your breath serves as an anchor to the present moment and a way to gauge regulation. Throughout Received Self-Regulation, you're aware of your breath. Is it calm? Shallow? Fast? Slow? In your belly or chest? You're not controlling your breath (unless you need to re-anchor), but you're staying connected to it. If you lose connection with your breath, it indicates you might be losing your anchoring in safety.

blocks.p: Staying connected to your breath is primarily an intentional check-in. However, it can also involve a deliberate, larger inhalation to re-regulate if you notice yourself losing access to safety. Ideally, you are deeply aligned with your body's natural breathing. When your body holds its breath, perhaps due to an increase in freeze, you stay with it, trusting that your body will take another breath. Ideally, you remain with it long enough for your body to spontaneously take a larger, natural breath without conscious effort.

ol: As the Mindful Conduit, you also need to assess when to continue and when to pause: You may need to pause the practice based on the [four "When to Stop" signs](piece:starting-and-stopping#when-to-stop). Received Self-Regulation should be at least manageable, but it can also be one of the most beautiful experiences you've had (that isn't substance-induced), though experiences can vary greatly.

blocks.p: After serving as the Mindful Conduit for Received self-regulation, you may feel relief, lightness, or a sense that something has shifted or been released. Your sense of self, your connection to the internal and external worlds, your purpose, and the meaning of life... everything feels different. At least, for now. This awareness of your place in reality isn't permanent, but it can linger.

Received self-regulation requires trust. Trust in your body, the process, and yourself. This can be hard, especially if you've spent years not trusting your body. Received self-regulation requires a different relationship with your body. It requires recognizing that your body is not your enemy: it's your ally. It's been trying to protect you, keep you safe, and help you survive. And now, given the right conditions, it's trying to heal.

Your body knows how to self-regulate. It's hardwired for it. Every living organism has this capacity. What's been missing is the safety, permission, and capacity to let it happen. You've built that through your practice. Now you need to trust that your body knows what to do.

blocks.why: Received self-regulation grows out of the active kind. This practice is the active kind, at your pace.

blocks.p: Trust sounds like:

ul: "My body knows more than my thinking mind."
"I don't have to control this; I just have to allow it."
"I've done the preparation. My body is ready."

blocks.p: Trust doesn't mean blind faith. You're not abandoning your discernment or ignoring warning signs. You're still checking in, still monitoring your safety anchoring, still recognizing when to pause. But within that framework of safety and awareness, you're trusting your body's wisdom to guide the process.
"I'm not experiencing any spontaneous shifts."

Received Self-Regulation requires significant groundwork. Have the skills truly become [second nature](piece:second-nature-and-alignment)? Is your thinking in sync with your body (what I call [Alignment](piece:second-nature-and-alignment#alignment))? If you answered "no" to any of these, return to Active self-regulation practice. Received can't be forced.
"I think something is happening, but I'm not sure if it's self-regulation or just me feeling things."

It's likely you're "just feeling things," though keep in mind the body is always trying to self-regulate, so it's happening to some degree. It might be an emotion that needs your attention or maybe an Obstacle.
"Received self-regulation seems to only happen during deep sessions, not in daily life."

Yep. Received typically occurs during dedicated meditation practice when you have time, space, and strong safety anchoring. The benefit for daily life comes indirectly: as your baseline defensive activation decreases through these sessions, daily life becomes easier. As you practice, you'll notice small moments when your body regulates when you pay attention without doing anything special.
"I had one experience of spontaneous shifts, but now nothing is happening again."

Received self-regulation isn't constant. It emerges when your nervous system has something ready to process, and the conditions are right. You might have one profound session followed by weeks of "normal" Active practice. This doesn't mean you regressed. Your body may have processed what it needed to.

Received Self-Regulation is what becomes available through consistent Active Self-Regulation: spontaneous state shifts, physical releases, and impulses that surface as your body's innate wisdom takes over, characterized by self-regulation happening through you rather than as something you do.

Your role shifts from active practitioner to witness and experiencer. Maintain safety anchoring and conscious awareness while allowing your body's process to unfold, trusting its wisdom rather than trying to control it.
Common experiences include state shifts, physical Sensations, Emotional transformations, and Impulses arising.
Intentionally practice [Balancing or Pendulating](piece:balancing-and-pendulating), then [Hold and Watch](piece:holding-and-watching) to open the potential for Received self-regulation.

blocks.prompt: Have you noticed any spontaneous self-regulation shifts during or after practice?
Are you able to maintain safety anchoring while allowing your body's process to unfold?
Can you distinguish between "doing" and "allowing" during practice?
